newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria rebels kill more than 80 villagers - papers.
newsitem.headline: Algeria rebels kill more than 80 villagers - papers.

text.p: Algerian Moslem rebels armed with swords and guns slaughtered more than 80 villagers in two attacks in hamlets south of Algiers, national newspapers said on Saturday.
The latest massacres in the remote hamlets coincided with a flare-up of violence in Algiers with rebels ambushing police patrols and detonating a bomb outside a restaurant in the crowded city.

A newspaper also reported the security forces have killed 30 guerrillas in a raid against one of their strongholds to bring the number of rebels killed in the past month according to the press to more than 300.

Scores of rebels armed with guns and swords killed 38 villagers in Sidi el Madani hamlet in Blida province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, overnight Thursday-Friday, El Watan and Al Khabar newspapers said.
Forty-three people were killed in a similar raid by Moslem guerrillas in Metmata village in Ain Defla province, 120 km (75 miles) southwest of Algiers, overnight Tuesday-Wednesday, they said.
Among the dead were elderly men, women and children, the newspapers added.
"(The assailants) raided Sidi el Madani village and left corpses of women, children and elderly villagers lying in a pool of blood," El Watan said.
The rebels wounded 12 other villagers as they were escaping the massacre, it added.
They decimated whole families in the raid, including children under six, Al Khabar said.
Between 40 and 60 rebels attacked Metmata village overnight Tuesday-Wednesday killing 41 people by cutting their throats or shooting them by guns, El Watan and Al Khabar said.
The guerrillas kidnapped four girls, two of them were found later dead with their throats slashed, they added.
Among the victims in Metmata were 11 children and seven women, two of them pregnant, Al Khabar said.
The newspaper named a man, Ahmed Menal, who lost 25 family members and relatives in the raid. The guerrillas shot him in the face and then cut his throat.
"Terrorist activities witnessed a worrying increase in the past weeks giving an impression of a return to square one of the first years of terrorism in Algeria," the influential El Watan said.
About 60,000 people died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.

The authorities, trying to play down setbacks dealt to them by the Moslem guerrillas, had said the conflict caught the unprepared government forces by surprise but they assured later that the government had the upper hand over the guerrillas.

Rebels killed four policemen in an ambush in La Glaciere suburb, south of Algiers, on Wedensday, El Watan said. A fifth policeman was shot dead in a similar attack in the neighbouring Bachdjarah surbub.

El Watan said more than 50 cars were reported stolen recently by suspected members of the feared Islamic Armed Group (GIA) in the aim to ladden them with explosives and unleash a wave of bombings in the Algerian capital.
On Wednesday a car bomb outside a restaurant in Algiers killed eight people and wounded 25, ending a more than two-week lull in bombings in the capital.

The authorities blame the GIA on the massacres of villagers and deadly bombings, mainly in Algiers. Newspapers said the GIA stepped up massacres and other killings in the past weeks in revenge for a military offensive in which up to 300 rebels were killed south of Algiers.
More than 30 GIA's members were killed in a new government force raid against a GIA stronghold in Sidi Bouzid village, in Blida province, Al Khabar said.
Al Khabar did not said when the guerrillas were killed but said the raid by the government troops ended on Thursday.
